pages.title: VLF withstand
pages.for: Is the insulation sound above its working stress? Hold an AC overvoltage at 0.1 Hz for a set time, before the cable is energised.
pages.rule:
Xc = 1 ÷ 2πfC
I = V ÷ Xc = 2πfCV
Test voltage = the spec's multiple × U0
Peak = rms × 1.4142

U0: core to earth, the first number of the rating.
One range in use: 1.5 to 2.5 U0. The spec decides.
IEEE, installation and acceptance: under 2 to 3 U0. Maintenance: about 75%.
At 0.1 Hz: 60 min on new cable, 30 min for a simple withstand on aged cable.
Check the set: peak within its kV peak, core µF within its rating at your frequency.
Rated above 35 kV: ends may need terminations against flashover.
Rated above 36 kV: a spec may ask for a resonant test at 10 to 500 Hz.
Pass: no breakdown for the full time.

pages.name: Do you still have it?
pages.task: What VLF test voltage range applies to a 12/20 kV cable?
pages.alt: The range is 1.5 to 2.5 U0. U0 is the voltage from each core to earth, the first number in 12/20 kV. 1.5 × 12 = 18.0 kV, and 2.5 × 12 = 30.0 kV. The 30 to 50 kV answer uses 20 kV, the voltage between cores. The 12 to 20 kV answer is the rating itself, with no overvoltage.
pages.html:
The range is 1.5 to 2.5 U0. U0 is the voltage from each core to earth, the first number in 12/20 kV. 1.5 × 12 = 18.0 kV, and 2.5 × 12 = 30.0 kV.

The 30 to 50 kV answer uses 20 kV, the voltage between cores. The 12 to 20 kV answer is the rating itself, with no overvoltage.

pages.name: What it is for
pages.text:
The VLF test is a pressure test. It holds an AC overvoltage on the insulation for a set time. The IR test checked the XLPE at 5 kV d.c. This test stresses it above its working voltage. It runs before the cable is energised.

Take a defect bad enough to spark at the test voltage. The small discharges inside it are partial discharges. They start an electrical tree. That is a set of fine breakdown channels that branch out through the XLPE. The tree grows until the core breaks down, during the test. Smaller defects are not affected. So a pass means the core held the voltage for the full time with no breakdown. That gives a high chance the insulation is sound. It does not prove there are no defects at all.

Not every spec uses VLF. On a submarine cable rated above 36 kV, the spec may ask for an AC test at 10 to 500 Hz, from a resonant test set. The client's spec decides.

If it is skipped

Skip it, and a defect the test would have found stays in the cable. It is still there when the cable is switched on.

pages.name: The why: 0.1 Hz
pages.text: Each core is a capacitor, as in lesson 1. Conductor and screen are the plates. String B's core is 0.528 µF. To hold an AC voltage on it, the test set fills it with charge, empties it, and fills it the other way, every cycle. That flow of charge is the charging current. The charge in each cycle is set by the capacitance and the voltage. The frequency sets how often it flows. One cycle at 0.1 Hz takes 10 s. In those 10 s, 50 Hz runs 50 × 10 = 500 cycles. So at 50 Hz the set moves the same charge 500 times as often, and the current is 500 times bigger. At 50 Hz one core of String B needs 12.61 A at 76 kV. The set supplies 958.4 kVA. Each step down cuts the current in proportion. At 0.1 Hz the same voltage needs 25.21 mA and 1.92 kVA. That is 500 times less, because the core goes through 500 times fewer cycles. That is the reactance at work. Xc = 1 ÷ 2πfC, so dropping f from 50 Hz to 0.1 Hz raises Xc 50 ÷ 0.1 = 500 times. The current is I = V ÷ Xc = 2πfCV, so it falls 500 times. The power the set supplies, V × I, falls with it.
pages.alt: Step the frequency down from 50 Hz to 0.1 Hz. VOLTAGE ON ONE CORE: 76 KV RMS AT EVERY FREQUENCY 0 peak 107.5 kV 1 cycle in 10 s 0 2 4 6 8 10 s Charging current 0.1 Hz 25.21 mA 50 Hz 12.61 A Charging current 25.21 mA Set supplies 1.92 kVA At 0.1 Hz the core goes through one cycle in 10 s. The same 76 kV takes 25.21 mA, 500 times less than at 50 Hz. The set supplies 1.92 kVA. That is the reactance at work. Xc = 1 ÷ 2πfC, so dropping f from 50 Hz to 0.1 Hz raises Xc 50 ÷ 0.1 = 500 times. The current is I = V ÷ Xc = 2πfCV, so it falls 500 times. The power the set supplies, V × I, falls with it.
pages.html:
Step the frequency down from 50 Hz to 0.1 Hz.

Voltage on one core: 76 kV rms at every frequency

Charging current25.21 mA
Set supplies1.92 kVA

At 0.1 Hz the core goes through one cycle in 10 s. The same 76 kV takes 25.21 mA, 500 times less than at 50 Hz. The set supplies 1.92 kVA.

That is the reactance at work. Xc = 1 ÷ 2πfC, so dropping f from 50 Hz to 0.1 Hz raises Xc 50 ÷ 0.1 = 500 times. The current is I = V ÷ Xc = 2πfCV, so it falls 500 times. The power the set supplies, V × I, falls with it.

pages.name: The why: long cables and the set
pages.text: A VLF set is rated by the capacitance it can drive at each frequency. Take a set that drives 0.75 µF at 0.1 Hz, 1.5 µF at 0.05 Hz and 3.75 µF at 0.02 Hz, up to 200 kV peak. It is a practice set, modelled on a real one. Use the rating of the set in front of you. The set can only supply so much current. Halve the frequency and each microfarad takes half the current. So the same set drives twice the capacitance. A core's capacitance grows with its length. So a long cable may need a lower frequency, a lower voltage, or both. 0.1 Hz is the standard. Go lower only when the cable is too big a load for the set at 0.1 Hz. The recommended test times are for 0.1 Hz. String B's 2.40 km core is 0.528 µF. That is inside the set's 0.75 µF, so it tests at 0.1 Hz. Past about 3.41 km a core is too big for the set at 0.1 Hz, so it drops to 0.05 Hz. Past about 6.82 km it drops to 0.02 Hz. At 8.0 km the core is 1.760 µF. Why not DC? Once a cable is charged, DC needs almost no current. But DC can leave space charge in XLPE. That is charge trapped in the insulation itself. This trapped charge can speed up water trees in healthy XLPE. Standards now discourage DC withstand tests on XLPE. VLF reverses the polarity every cycle. That cuts the build-up. It is still a compromise. 0.1 Hz does not stress the XLPE exactly as 50 Hz will in service.

So the same set drives twice the capacitance. A core's capacitance grows with its length. So a long cable may need a lower frequency, a lower voltage, or both. 0.1 Hz is the standard.

It is a practice set, modelled on a real one. Use the rating of the set in front of you. The set can only supply so much current. Halve the frequency and each microfarad takes half the current. Core capacitance1.760 µF
Frequency the set can use0.02 Hz

An 8.0 km core is 1.760 µF. That is more than the set's 1.5 µF at 0.05 Hz. At 0.02 Hz the set drives 3.75 µF, so it tests at 0.02 Hz.

Why not DC?

Once a cable is charged, DC needs almost no current. But DC can leave space charge in XLPE. That is charge trapped in the insulation itself. This trapped charge can speed up water trees in healthy XLPE. Standards now discourage DC withstand tests on XLPE. VLF reverses the polarity every cycle. That cuts the build-up. It is still a compromise. 0.1 Hz does not stress the XLPE exactly as 50 Hz will in service.

pages.name: Check
pages.task: You test String B's core at the same 76 kV, but drop the set from 0.1 Hz to 0.05 Hz. What does the charging current do?
pages.alt: Half the frequency doubles Xc. The current is V ÷ Xc, so it halves: 25.21 ÷ 2 = 12.61 mA. That is why the set drives twice the capacitance at 0.05 Hz.
pages.html: Half the frequency doubles Xc. The current is V ÷ Xc, so it halves: 25.21 ÷ 2 = 12.61 mA. That is why the set drives twice the capacitance at 0.05 Hz.

pages.name: Worked example
pages.text: A new cable rated 12/20 kV, tested for installation. On a 12/20 kV cable, U0 is 12 kV. So 1.5 to 2.5 U0 is 18.0 to 30.0 kV rms. A new cable holds the spec's level at 0.1 Hz for 60 minutes. It passes if there is no breakdown. Then discharge it in order: display, discharge stick, hook, hand earth. Earths then go on core and screen at both ends, and stay on.
pages.alt: 1 Before you start: identify, isolate, prove dead, secure and earth. Disconnect the circuit, with no monitoring equipment left on it. Restrict access at both ends. Use only the maker's test leads. 2 U0 is the rated voltage from each core to earth or screen. In 12/20 kV it is the first number: U0 = 12 kV. 3 Lowest level: 1.5 × U0 = 1.5 × 12 = 18.0 kV. 4 Highest level: 2.5 × U0 = 2.5 × 12 = 30.0 kV. So the range is 18.0 to 30.0 kV rms. The client's spec picks the level. 5 A new cable on installation: 0.1 Hz for 60 minutes. A simple withstand on aged cable would run 30 minutes.
pages.html:
1

Before you start: identify, isolate, prove dead, secure and earth. Disconnect the circuit, with no monitoring equipment left on it. Restrict access at both ends. Use only the maker's test leads.

2

U0 is the rated voltage from each core to earth or screen. In 12/20 kV it is the first number: U0 = 12 kV.

3

Lowest level: 1.5 × U0 = 1.5 × 12 = 18.0 kV.

4

Highest level: 2.5 × U0 = 2.5 × 12 = 30.0 kV. So the range is 18.0 to 30.0 kV rms. The client's spec picks the level.

5

A new cable on installation: 0.1 Hz for 60 minutes. A simple withstand on aged cable would run 30 minutes.

6

It passes if the core holds the voltage for the full 60 minutes with no breakdown.

7

End of test: wait for the display to show discharged. Then apply the discharge stick, then the hook straight after it, then the hand earth. Earths go on core and screen at both ends, and stay on. Charge held in the XLPE can bring the voltage back for minutes or hours after the first discharge. Prove there is no voltage before anyone touches the cable.

Specs differ on the range. One range in use is 1.5 to 2.5 U0. IEEE puts installation and acceptance from under 2 U0 up to 3 U0. IEEE maintenance tests run at about 75% of that. The client's spec sets the level on the job. String B is 38/66 kV, so U0 = 38 kV. For String B, 1.5 to 2.5 U0 is 57.0 to 95.0 kV.

Give it in kV, to 1 place.

Test voltage = 2 × U0

= 2 × 38 = 76.0 kV rms

76.0 kV rms is 2 U0, which sits inside 57.0 to 95.0 kV. Sets are rated in kV peak. Peak = rms × 1.4142. So the set must reach 76 × 1.4142 = 107.5 kV peak. The practice set's 200 kV peak covers it. On a cable rated above 35 kV, the ends may need terminations fitted to stop flashover.

pages.name: Section B
pages.task: Explain why VLF is used rather than a 50 Hz test on a long cable.
pages.why: A model answer: A long cable is a large capacitance. At 50 Hz its reactance is low. So holding a withstand voltage on it needs a very large charging current and a lot of power. That often makes a 50 Hz set impractical on site. Lowering the frequency raises the reactance, so the current and power fall with the frequency. At 0.1 Hz they are 500 times less than at 50 Hz. So a set you can take to site can do the test. It still holds an AC overvoltage. A defect bad enough to spark at the test voltage grows to failure during the test. DC would need even less current. But it can leave space charge in XLPE. Standards now discourage DC withstand tests on XLPE. VLF keeps an alternating test. Its changing polarity cuts that build-up.

pages.name: Changed numbers
pages.task: Another core of the same cable type runs 3.10 km. It is tested at 76 kV and 0.1 Hz. Determine its charging current.
pages.alt: Same method, new numbers. These are practice values. Give it in mA, to 2 places. C = 0.22 × 3.10 = 0.682 µF I = 2πfCV = 2π × 0.1 × 0.682 × 10⁻⁶ × 76 000 = 32.57 mA 0.682 µF is inside the practice set's 0.75 µF at 0.1 Hz, so 0.1 Hz still works.
